That means, if I have a triangle ABC, then angle A plus angle B should be less than 180 degrees, right? Because two right angles are 180 degrees each, so two right angles would be 360 degrees. Wait, that doesn't make sense because the sum of angles in a triangle is only 180 degrees. Maybe I'm misinterpreting it.

So, maybe it's saying that for any two angles in the triangle, their sum is less than 180 degrees. That makes more sense because if all three angles add up to 180, then any two of them would indeed be less than 180.

Okay, so how do I prove that? Well, first, I know that in any triangle, the sum of all three angles is 180 degrees. So if I have angles A, B, and C, then A + B + C = 180 degrees. But wait, the problem says "taken together in any possible way." So I guess I need to show that not only for A and B, but also for A and C, and B and C, their sums are each less than 180 degrees. Using the same logic, since all angles are positive and their total is 180, each pair's sum should be less than 180. That checks out.

Maybe I should also think about what would happen if one angle is 90 degrees or more. If, for example, angle A is 90 degrees, then angles B and C must add up to 90 degrees. So B + C = 90, which is still less than 180. If angle A is, say, 100 degrees, then B + C would be 80 degrees. Still less than 180. No matter how I adjust the angles, as long as their total is 180, any two will always be less than 180.

I guess this is a fundamental property of triangles. It might relate to the concept of triangle inequality, where the sum of any two sides must be greater than the third side. To make sure I'm not missing anything, maybe I should consider different types of triangles: acute, right, and obtuse. In an acute triangle, all angles are less than 90 degrees, so any two angles would definitely add up to less than 180. In a right triangle, one angle is exactly 90 degrees, so the other two must add up to 90 degrees. Again, any two angles would sum to less than 180. In an obtuse triangle, one angle is greater than 90 degrees, but the other two must still add up to less than 90 degrees to keep the total at 180. So in all cases, the sum of any two angles is less than 180 degrees.

theorem any_two_angles_sum_less_two_right_angles (a b c : Point) (AB BC AC : Line) (h : formTriangle a b c AB BC AC) : (∠ a:b:c + ∠ b:c:a) < ∟ + ∟ ∧ (∠ a:c:b + ∠ b:c:a) < ∟ + ∟ ∧ (∠ a:b:c + ∠ a:c:b) < ∟ + ∟ := by
  -- Establish the sum of angles in a triangle as 180 degrees.
  have h₁ : (∠ a:b:c + ∠ b:c:a + ∠ a:c:b) = ∟ + ∟ := by
    apply TriangleAngles.sum
    exact h
  -- Prove each pair of angles sums to less than 180 degrees.
  refine' ⟨by linarith [h₁], by linarith [h₁], by linarith [h₁]⟩

nl_statement: For any triangle,  (the sum of) two angles taken together in any (possible way) is less than two right-angles. Let $ABC$ be a triangle. I say that (the sum of) two angles of triangle $ABC$ taken together in any (possible way) is less than two right-angles. <prf> Thus, (the sum of) $ABC$ and $BCA$ is less than two right-angles. Similarly, we can show that (the sum of) $BAC$ and $ACB$ is also less than two right-angles, and further (that the sum of) $CAB$ and $ABC$ (is less than two right-angles).Thus, for any triangle,  (the sum of) two angles taken together in any (possible way) is less than two right-angles.
